strengths: The central idea is original and relevant: using a pretrained multi-view diffusion model both to synthesize supervisory views and to provide features that are unprojected into an explicit 3D volume offers a plausible route to learning from collections of single images.

The method combines differentiable volumetric keypoint extraction, projection-based reconstruction, learned connectivity, and downstream rigging into a coherent framework. Predicting connectivity in addition to points increases its potential usefulness for animation and manipulation.

The Human3.6M results provide meaningful evidence that the representation encodes 3D pose. With 18 discovered keypoints and a two-layer regressor, the method obtains 121.34 MPJPE and 85.26 P-MPJPE, improving over the listed single-view version of Honari et al. and BKinD-3D with two real views on the reported metrics.

The ablations support two important design choices: replacing diffusion features with per-view ResNet features worsens P-MPJPE from 85.26 to 101.55, while increasing generated views from one to four improves MPJPE from 166.29 to 121.34.

The qualitative results span humans, unseen dog breeds, other animal species, and scanned objects, and the manuscript clearly acknowledges dependence on diffusion quality, computational cost, and object-centric masking.
weaknesses: The evidence is substantially narrower than the claims of accurate, arbitrary-category, and exceptional out-of-domain 3D keypoint estimation. Quantitative 3D evaluation is restricted to Human3.6M; Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, GSO, and the animation application are assessed only through selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative test of cross-species consistency, 3D accuracy, connectivity, or deformation quality.

The headline comparison is not fully supported. The paper states that it outperforms all unsupervised single-view baselines, but Table 1 reports Kundu et al. at 99.2 MPJPE versus 121.34 for the proposed method on the full protocol. Moreover, the methods use different auxiliary supervision and priors, so the comparison needs more careful qualification.

Labeling the proposed method as using one view in Table 1 is potentially misleading: it observes one real image but generates and processes four views at inference. This still qualifies as monocular input, yet its computational information path and cost differ materially from feed-forward single-view baselines and should be represented explicitly.

The Human3.6M training protocol leaves a possible confound. Treating frames independently does not establish that synchronized views of the same poses were excluded from the training collection. Even without using their correspondence, repeated poses from a calibrated multi-camera capture distribution weaken the claimed demonstration of learning from unconstrained single-view collections.

Several details needed to assess or reproduce the method are absent: architectures for the aggregation, volumetric, appearance, and reconstruction networks; the affine-augmentation distribution; adjacency parameterization and regularization; exact differentiable line construction; attention tensor semantics in Eq. 4; MST cost definition; view/camera selection; and inference time and memory. A promise to release code does not resolve these omissions in the submitted manuscript.

The training objective is insufficiently analyzed for identifiability. Appearance features may let the reconstruction network bypass the keypoints, while the mask loss constrains only the aggregate edge map. There are no ablations for the reconstruction and mask losses, random affine transformation, learned adjacency, or appearance pathway, and no measurements of keypoint diversity or collapse.

The animation contribution is only demonstrated qualitatively and appears to rely substantially on an external multi-view reconstruction pipeline. No baseline, failure analysis, deformation metric, or evaluation of whether the learned MST corresponds to articulation is provided.

Presentation refinements include defining whether softmax view weights in Eq. 4 are computed per keypoint channel, correcting minor notation and grammar issues, and avoiding language such as “exceptional generalization” when the evidence is qualitative. These are secondary to the evaluation and reproducibility concerns above.

strengths: The central idea—turning intermediate features from a pretrained multi-view diffusion model into an explicit 3D feature volume for unsupervised keypoint discovery—is interesting and potentially useful. The integration of generated views, calibrated unprojection, volumetric heatmaps, and reconstruction supervision is a coherent contribution.

The Human3.6M results provide some evidence that the discovered representation contains 3D pose information. With 18 keypoints and a two-layer regressor, the method improves over the cited single-view Honari et al. baseline from 125.73/121.04/89.05 to 121.34/118.29/85.26 MPJPE/N-MPJPE/P-MPJPE.
The ablations show meaningful gains from diffusion features over the stated ResNet alternative and a consistent improvement as additional virtual views are introduced.

The paper considers humans, dogs, unseen animal species, and object manipulation; the qualitative results suggest that the approach may transfer beyond its quantitative human-pose setting. weaknesses: The empirical evidence is substantially narrower than the claims. Quantitative evaluation is confined to Human3.6M, while accuracy and generalization on Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, and GSO are supported only by a few selected examples. There is no quantitative cross-category consistency, landmark quality, or failure-rate evaluation, so claims of exceptional generalization across arbitrary categories are not established.

The animatable-object contribution is especially under-validated. It is demonstrated through limited qualitative examples without comparison to rigging or deformation baselines, quantitative deformation measures, a user study, or evaluation over a meaningful test set. The results therefore establish feasibility rather than reliable manipulation quality.

The claimed supervision setting needs sharper qualification. Although the task-specific model does not consume captured multi-view tuples, both its inference features and training targets come from SV3D-p, a pretrained multi-view model that encodes multi-view data and camera supervision. Describing the overall approach simply as learning “without multi-view supervision” obscures this inherited supervision and complicates comparison with methods trained from scratch.

Important possible degeneracies are not ruled out. The reconstruction network receives appearance features that could bypass the keypoint representation, while the mask loss directly encourages a maximum over dense keypoint-pair lines to cover the silhouette. The paper provides no ablations for the reconstruction pathway, appearance conditioning, mask loss, affine augmentation, learned adjacency, or edge-map construction, and does not demonstrate that the learned graph is necessary rather than incidental.

Several comparisons are difficult to interpret because methods use different numbers of discovered keypoints, different regressors, different auxiliary priors, and in one case a six-action subset. The proposed method only modestly improves the closest reported single-view baseline and remains clearly behind the strongest multi-view result. Variance across runs and statistical uncertainty are also absent.

Core technical and reproducibility details are missing: SV3D camera sampling and input-camera alignment, canonical-volume extent and scale, visibility and out-of-frame handling during unprojection, the precise view-attention operation in Eq. 4, selected U-Net layers and feature dimensions, architectures of the volumetric and reconstruction networks, appearance extraction, affine parameters, and the adjacency/MST weighting and skinning hyperparameters. No code is supplied with the reviewed manuscript, only a promise of future release.

The cost and practical meaning of “monocular” inference are insufficiently characterized. Each prediction invokes multi-view diffusion generation or denoising and volumetric processing, yet runtime, memory, stochastic variability, and sensitivity to diffusion seeds or generated-view failures are not measured. The view-count ablation also jointly changes available geometry and computation rather than isolating their effects.

The qualitative human visualizations show raw discovered graphs that are not obviously anatomically aligned with the displayed ground truth, while quantitative scores are obtained only after fitting a supervised regressor on ground-truth 3D poses. The paper should more clearly separate intrinsic semantic keypoint discovery from downstream decodability; as presented, the evidence supports the latter more strongly than the former. Overall, the promising idea and initial Human3.6M result are outweighed by under-supported breadth claims, insufficient controls, and limited reproducibility, leading to a weak-reject recommendation rather than a categorical rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored setting: discovering monocular 3D keypoints without target-domain keypoint annotations, calibrated captures, or real multi-view training sets.

The core design is coherent and original in its combination: SV3D-p supplies synthetic views and geometry-aware intermediate features, which are unprojected into a 3D volume and trained through differentiable projection and reconstruction.

Human3.6M results support the method's practical value. With 18 keypoints and the MLP regressor, it obtains 121.34 MPJPE and 85.26 P-MPJPE, improving over the reported single-view KeypointNet and Honari et al. results and surpassing the reported two-view BKinD-3D result.

The ablations provide useful evidence for two central choices. Diffusion features improve P-MPJPE from 101.55 to 85.26 relative to ResNet features, while increasing virtual views from one to four improves P-MPJPE from 104.22 to 85.26.

The framework is demonstrated across humans, dogs, unseen animal species, and non-human objects, and the alignment between its keypoints and diffusion coordinates enables an interesting automatic rigging and manipulation application.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually communicates the pipeline and qualitative behavior effectively.
weaknesses: Quantitative evidence is concentrated on Human3.6M. Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, DAVIS, GSO, cross-species generalization, and object manipulation are evaluated only through a small number of qualitative examples. This is insufficient to substantiate the strongest claims of exceptional generalization and broadly effective manipulation, particularly because AP-10K supplies annotations that could support quantitative evaluation.

The comparison table mixes materially different supervision, view counts, keypoint counts, regressors, and action subsets. The default method's improvement over the closest single-view Honari et al. result is modest, while the strongest four-view Honari result remains substantially better. The six-action result should not be compared directly with full-dataset results.

Calling the approach free of multi-view supervision requires qualification: target-domain training uses independent images, but the method depends centrally on a pretrained multi-view diffusion model whose learned geometric prior derives from multi-view/3D training data. It also generates and consumes four virtual views at inference, so the contribution is best characterized as single-image input rather than purely single-view computation.

The evaluation learns linear or nonlinear mappings from discovered keypoints to ground-truth joints. Although standard, the two-hidden-layer MLP can absorb nonlinear discrepancies and does not by itself demonstrate semantic correspondence or stable keypoint identity. Direct consistency, repeatability, or correspondence metrics would strengthen this claim.

Several implementation-critical elements are underspecified: the reconstruction and appearance networks, diffusion sampling procedure, volume bounds and coordinate normalization, view-attention computation, adjacency constraints, construction and width of Gaussian edge maps, foreground-mask generation for synthesized views, and the exact combination of edge weights and distance used by the MST. The promised code is not part of the submitted evidence.

The training objective lacks ablations for reconstruction, mask, affine augmentation, learned connectivity, diffusion timestep/layers, and volume resolution. Consequently, the evidence does not isolate several claimed mechanisms or rule out an appearance shortcut in the reconstruction network.

Computational cost is acknowledged but not measured. Running diffusion denoising, processing multiple generated views, and constructing 72-cubed volumes is likely expensive; runtime, memory, sampling variance, and comparison with feed-forward alternatives are important for assessing usefulness and reproducibility.

Some mathematical descriptions need clarification. In particular, the view-attention softmax in Eq. 4 is applied to vector-valued keypoint features without defining whether weights are scalar or keypoint-specific, and the dense adjacency matrix's symmetry, normalization, and role in differentiable line construction are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper studies an important and relatively underexplored problem: category-flexible 3D keypoint discovery when only one image is supplied to the system. Using a pretrained multi-view diffusion model to create virtual views and expose geometry-aware intermediate features is a sensible and reasonably original direction.

The proposed pipeline is coherent at a high level: multi-layer diffusion features are fused, unprojected into a voxel volume, and decoded into differentiable 3D keypoints. Predicting keypoints directly from the volume performs materially better than the reported 2D-keypoint-plus-triangulation variant (85.26 versus 93.68 P-MPJPE).

The Human3.6M experiments provide evidence that the learned representation is useful. With the standard downstream MLP regressor, the method improves over the listed single-view Honari et al. result from 125.73 to 121.34 MPJPE and from 89.05 to 85.26 P-MPJPE, despite using fewer discovered keypoints in its default configuration.

The ablations cover several meaningful design choices, including feature backbone, number of generated views, diffusion timestep, training-set size, affine augmentation, lifting strategy, view misalignment, and keypoint count. In particular, the comparisons against ResNet50, CLIP, and DINOv2 support the value of SV3D features rather than merely the volumetric architecture.

The authors clearly disclose important limitations, including left-right ambiguity, failures inherited from inconsistent diffusion generations, and the very high computational cost of SV3D. The supplement also gives useful architecture and runtime details.

The demonstrations across humans, birds, dogs, and unseen animals suggest potentially useful category generalization, while the mesh-rigging application illustrates a plausible downstream use of the discovered structure.
weaknesses: The central claim that Human3.6M training and evaluation require no manual annotations is contradicted by the preprocessing described in the supplement. Human3.6M foreground masks are produced by prompting SAM with provided 2D keypoint locations, and crops are computed from bounding boxes enclosing all projected 2D keypoints. This uses manual pose annotations, including during evaluation, and provides strong object localization. Because Human3.6M is the only benchmark with quantitative 3D evaluation, this materially undermines the claimed annotation-free setting and makes comparison with differently preprocessed baselines difficult to interpret.

The evidence for the broad claim of accurate 3D keypoints across arbitrary categories is limited. Animals and out-of-domain categories receive no quantitative 3D evaluation; CUB is evaluated only after 2D projection, and on CUB-all with four keypoints the method is worse than StableKeypoints (7.7 versus 5.4). The generalization figures contain selected qualitative examples without a specified sampling protocol, consistency metric, or comparison.

Some essential technical definitions are incomplete or questionable. Equation 4 defines a scalar attention weight as a softmax over feature tensors without specifying the scoring function or the dimensions over which softmax operates. More seriously, the supplemental view-invariant loss compares projections before and after randomly rotating the 3D feature volume directly; as written, it enforces invariance rather than transforming one prediction back or enforcing equivariance. This makes the animal-training objective difficult to reproduce and raises the possibility of an incorrectly stated or degenerative constraint.

The Human3.6M gains over the most relevant single-view discovery baseline are modest, and no multi-run variance or statistical uncertainty is reported. Comparisons also mix different keypoint counts, regressors, training supervision, and in one case a simplified action subset. Consequently, the tables provide less decisive evidence than the accompanying claims suggest.

The animatable-object contribution is supported only by a few qualitative examples. There is no comparison against automatic rigging alternatives, no deformation or correspondence metric, and no evaluation of artifacts under substantial articulation. The MST construction is also not reproducibly specified: the paper says it combines learned edge weights and Euclidean distances but does not give the actual cost function or coefficients.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplemental architecture description. The manuscript does not fully specify the diffusion sampling and feature extraction procedure, the precise attention computation, heatmap construction, appearance encoder, regression training protocol, MST objective, or selection protocol for qualitative examples. No code or trained-model availability is stated.

Inference is extremely expensive: the diffusion stage requires about 29.5 GB of VRAM and 11.9 seconds per example on an A6000, roughly 7.8 TFLOPs. This does not invalidate the method, but substantially limits its practical usefulness and should temper claims of scalability.

There are several overstatements and clarity issues. The method does use synthetic multi-view supervision and inherits multi-view training priors from SV3D, so claims of operating “without multi-view supervision” require careful qualification. The paper also alternates between describing the input as unconstrained and relying on object-centric segmentation/cropping, including class-name prompts and ground-truth human keypoints. These are material scope issues, not merely presentation refinements.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and relatively underexplored problem: category-flexible 3D keypoint discovery when only a single image is available at test time.

Combining intermediate SV3D features, camera-aware volumetric unprojection, and differentiable keypoint extraction is technically sensible. The ablations support the use of diffusion features: SV3D features obtain 85.26 P-MPJPE versus 101.55–103.13 for ResNet50, DINOv2, and CLIP features.

The Human3.6M experiments include several relevant metrics and comparisons. The method improves over the reported single-view keypoint-discovery baselines, and the viewpoint-count, feature-backbone, lifting-strategy, timestep, and data-scale ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence.

The method is evaluated across humans, birds, and dogs, and the manuscript openly documents important failure modes, including left-right ambiguity and dependence on erroneous diffusion-generated views.
The animation application illustrates potential downstream usefulness beyond landmark evaluation, while the computational-cost table transparently reports the substantial diffusion overhead.
weaknesses: The central claim of annotation-free training is contradicted by the implementation. On Human3.6M, ground-truth 2D keypoints are used as SAM prompts and to construct tight person crops. These annotations affect both foreground extraction and spatial normalization, yet the paper repeatedly claims training without manual annotations. This is a material source of supervision and makes the primary 3D experiment insufficient evidence for the claimed setting.

The annotation issue extends to the animal evaluation: CUB-aligned preprocessing is landmark-based, while CUB-all uses provided bounding boxes. Consequently, none of the quantitative benchmarks cleanly demonstrates the advertised pipeline on unconstrained images without annotation-derived localization.

Evidence for category-generic 3D discovery is weak. Only Human3.6M has quantitative 3D evaluation. CUB is evaluated after projecting predictions to 2D, Stanford Dogs has no quantitative evaluation, and out-of-domain generalization is supported only by a small collection of qualitative examples. Plausible renderings do not establish accurate depth, cross-view consistency, or semantic correspondence.

Some conclusions overstate the tables. The paper says it outperforms all unsupervised single-view baselines, but Kundu et al. report 99.2 MPJPE versus 119.07 for the best full-set configuration here. On CUB-aligned, the method's 5.16 score is also worse than several originally published results; superiority is obtained only against the authors' reproductions under a separately sourced preprocessing pipeline whose comparability is difficult to verify.

The animation contribution is almost entirely qualitative. There are no baselines, deformation metrics, user study, or evaluation of mesh quality, skinning artifacts, and pose range. Two displayed examples are not sufficient to support claims of avoiding object-specific rigging across arbitrary categories.

Important design choices lack isolating ablations. In particular, the paper does not ablate the reconstruction loss, silhouette-mask loss, edge maps, learned adjacency, or random-affine shortcut prevention. It is therefore unclear which components prevent keypoint collapse or produce semantic structure. Forcing a maximum aggregation of Gaussian line segments toward a full foreground mask is also poorly justified.

The technical description is not fully reproducible. The view-attention equation applies a softmax directly to vector-valued features without defining how scalar or channel-wise weights are obtained; tensor shapes for the feature aggregator and keypoint head are inconsistent between the main paper and supplement; and the appearance encoder, generated-view mask extraction, affine-conditioning details, and stochastic inference protocol are underspecified.

The claimed monocular efficiency is impractical in the reported implementation: diffusion alone requires about 7,787 GFLOPs, 29.48 GB VRAM, and 11.93 seconds per image on an A6000. This does not invalidate the idea, but substantially limits usefulness and is not balanced by sufficiently strong quantitative gains.

Overall, the diffusion-based formulation is promising, but the annotation-dependent preprocessing directly compromises the submission's defining claim, while the animal, generalization, and animation claims remain largely qualitative. These concerns favor rejection despite the method's worthwhile technical direction.

strengths: The paper presents a novel and useful combination of pretrained multi-view diffusion features, differentiable unprojection, volumetric keypoint prediction, and reconstruction-based self-supervision. This directly addresses the difficult setting of learning monocular 3D keypoints without task-specific 3D pose labels or captured multi-view training sequences.

The Human3.6M results provide meaningful evidence: with 18 keypoints, the full-setting model obtains 121.34 MPJPE and 85.26 P-MPJPE using an MLP probe, outperforming the reported single-view unsupervised discovery baselines and some weaker multi-view configurations. The paper appropriately reports both linear and nonlinear probes rather than relying on only the more favorable mapping.

The ablations substantiate important design decisions. SV3D features outperform ResNet50, CLIP, and DINOv2 features; volumetric prediction improves over triangulated 2D keypoints; adding generated viewpoints produces a large gain; and supplementary experiments examine timestep, keypoint count, training-set size, affine augmentation, view misalignment, and aggregation.

The evaluation spans humans, birds, and dogs, while the qualitative results on DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K suggest encouraging transfer beyond the training distribution. The CUB study also makes a serious effort to reproduce baselines under consistent preprocessing and reports the discrepancy from their published numbers.

Predicting connectivity and aligning keypoints with the diffusion model's 3D coordinate system enables an interesting downstream rigging and manipulation application. The manuscript is generally clear, visually effective, and unusually candid about left-right ambiguity, diffusion failures, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The annotation-free claim is overstated for Human3.6M. The supplement states that ground-truth 2D keypoints are used as SAM prompts and to compute tight crops, including during evaluation. These are manual pose annotations and can supply strong localization information. Results with annotation-free masks and crops are needed to establish the claimed setting; at minimum, the claim and comparison protocol should explicitly acknowledge this dependence.

Evidence for category-general 3D discovery is limited. Only Human3.6M has quantitative 3D evaluation; CUB is evaluated after projection to 2D, Stanford Dogs is qualitative, and cross-category generalization is illustrated with a small number of selected examples. Thus the broad claims about accurate 3D structure and arbitrary categories are not fully verified.

The animation contribution is preliminary: only a few qualitative examples are shown, with visible deformation artifacts, and there is no quantitative evaluation or comparison for reconstruction quality, skeleton quality, skinning, or manipulation. It should be presented as a proof of concept rather than an established application advantage.

Reliance on SV3D complicates the supervision characterization: although KeyDiff3D itself does not consume captured multi-view images, it inherits geometric and data priors from a pretrained multi-view generator. The manuscript should more precisely distinguish task-training supervision from supervision embedded in the foundation model.

Inference is very expensive: the reported complete pipeline requires about 7,787 GFLOPs, 29.48 GB of VRAM, and 11.9 seconds per image, versus sub-second baselines. Moreover, reproducibility is weakened by unspecified details such as the selection of 8,800 Human3.6M frames, manual full-body filtering of Stanford Dogs, regression training settings, randomness, and variance across runs. These limitations are meaningful but do not outweigh the supported methodological contribution.
